summary: This document defines the standard format for sending mail messages between computers in the UUCP Project. It does not address how mail is stored on a machine or the lower-level transport. It sets a standard for hosts in the UUCP zone.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 976 explains how UUCP-connected computers should address and pass email to one another. It keeps the message headers in the Internet format while using UUCP paths to route the message between machines.

subtitle: How UUCP hosts carry Internet-style mail addresses without changing the message headers.

tldr.problem: UUCP hosts used bang-path addresses while Internet mail used user@domain addresses. Combining the forms could produce addresses with more than one interpretation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 976 adopts RFC 822 message headers and RFC 920 domain names, while keeping UUCP routing in the envelope and From_ lines. It describes rmail address forms and a routing method for hosts with different capabilities.
tldr.outcome: The memo sets a mail interchange format for the UUCP zone. The batch metadata says RFC 976 was updated by RFC 1137 and lists its status as Unknown.

today: RFC 976 was updated by RFC 1137; the batch metadata lists its status as Unknown. This memo defines a mail interchange format for UUCP hosts.

sections.title: Scope and Standards Adopted
sections.content:
RFC 976 defines a format for transmitting mail between machines in the UUCP Project. It does not define how a machine stores messages or the lower-level transport used between machines. It assumes remote execution of rmail, or an equivalent command.

To avoid creating another incompatible address format, the RFC adopts RFC 822 for mail messages and RFC 920 for domain names. It explains how to represent the envelope and route UUCP mail when systems have different capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo sets rules for email while it travels between UUCP computers. The message itself follows RFC 822, while UUCP routing information stays outside its ordinary headers.

sections.title: Message Parts and Address Forms
sections.content:
A mail item has an envelope and a message. The envelope carries destination addresses and a source path, usually in lines beginning From or >From . The RFC 822 headers and message body make up the message; intermediate hosts generally should not change them.

Older UUCP software uses bang paths such as a!b!c!user, while Internet-style addresses use user@domain. A mixed form such as a!b@c is ambiguous. The RFC recommends avoiding it and gives a consistent interpretation for systems that accept it.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope tells mail programs where a message is going and which machines passed it along. The headers and body are the message people read. Mixing the two address styles can leave a host unsure how to route mail.

sections.title: Sending Mail with rmail
sections.content:
A remote command should receive a message on standard input and an address such as rmail user@domain. More than one recipient may be supplied. The alternative rmail domain!user represents the same destination when the domain contains a period and no exclamation mark.

A route through older UUCP systems may use a sequence of bang-separated host names. The sender should avoid characters that intermediate systems may rewrite. Batch SMTP is an optional method: a host may treat mail to b-smtp as batched SMTP commands, with a leading hash on each line to protect the command stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending host gives rmail the recipient address and the message. If the next computer understands only older UUCP paths, the sender can express the route with exclamation marks instead.

sections.title: Routing Through Different Hosts
sections.content:
The RFC groups hosts into three classes. Class 1 handles local names and bang paths; Class 2 also understands some user@domain addresses; Class 3 can route for non-adjacent hosts and understand domain!user. A sender with no information about a host may treat it as Class 1.

To route an address, a host finds the most specific recognized domain suffix in its table, looks up a gateway and route, and selects the next directly connected host. It then chooses an address form that the next host can handle. When the sender is unsure about that host, the RFC recommends bang syntax where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail moves through one directly connected computer at a time. Each sender checks its routing table and uses an address form the next computer is expected to understand.

sections.title: Envelope and Header Requirements
sections.content:
Conforming hosts should accept local user names, bang paths, user@domain, domain!user, and the dotted form used for a domain with no periods. The envelope follows UUCP conventions and uses bang routing.

Header fields such as From: and To: must follow RFC 822, and header addresses must use the at-sign form. The originating site is responsible for making those addresses valid. A forwarding host must not turn a valid address into an invalid mixed address.
sections.plainLanguage: Use UUCP routing marks on the envelope and Internet-style addresses in the message headers. A computer passing the message along must not rewrite a valid header address into an invalid one.
